answer.label: Not Kahlil Gibran — actually Edwin Hubbell Chapin
answer.sourceLine: This line is from Chapin’s 1860 collection of sermons and addresses, Living Words, decades before Kahlil Gibran was even born. It is one of the most widely recirculated misattributions on quote sites today.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Out of suffering have emerged the strongest souls; the most massive characters are seamed with scars; martyrs have put on their coronation-robes glittering with fire, and through their tears have the sorrowful first seen the gates of heaven.
trail: First published in Edwin Hubbell Chapin’s Living Words ↗ (Boston: A. Tompkins, 1860).
Confirmed by full-text search of the original scanned volume, which locates the exact sentence on page 185 ↗.
Independently corroborated by Wikiquote's Edwin Hubbell Chapin page ↗, which cites the same 1860 source and page.
The Gibran misattribution is flagged on Wikiquote's Kahlil Gibran page ↗ under its Misattributed section.
source.excerptNote: The popular quote circulating online truncates this passage to its first clause and often alters “seamed” to “seared.”

sourceLink.text: Living Words at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: First published in 1860, over a century before the 1931 cutoff for automatic U.S. public-domain status, and Chapin died in 1880 — the text carries no surviving copyright.

author.name: Kahlil Gibran
author.heading: Kahlil Gibran
author.bio: Kahlil Gibran was a Lebanese-American writer and artist best known for The Prophet (1923), a collection of poetic essays that became one of the best-selling books of the twentieth century. Because his aphoristic style is so widely imitated, his name is frequently attached — wrongly — to sentimental lines he never wrote, including this one.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook case of a real 19th-century quotation drifting onto a more famous, unrelated name over a century later.

items.why: Quote-aggregator sites such as Goodreads, BrainyQuote, and QuoteFancy attribute the line to Gibran, and at least one blog claims (incorrectly) that it comes from The Prophet ↗; no such passage exists in that or any other Gibran work.
items.scope: Attributed the entire line to the wrong author and, in some cases, invented a source book for it.

misattribution.truthLine: Wikiquote lists the line under Gibran’s Misattributed section ↗, crediting it to Edwin Hubbell Chapin (as quoted in an 1895 quotation dictionary); Wikiquote’s own Chapin page ↗ traces it to his 1860 Living Words, p. 185.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: This inspirational line about suffering forging “the strongest souls” circulates on nearly every quote-aggregator site attributed to Kahlil Gibran, and is sometimes even claimed to come from The Prophet. It does not appear anywhere in Gibran’s actual writings.

The real author is Edwin Hubbell Chapin, a 19th-century American Universalist minister renowned in his day as a pulpit orator. The line comes from his 1860 book Living Words, a collection of his sermons and addresses, and originally continues: “…the most massive characters are seamed with scars; martyrs have put on their coronation-robes glittering with fire, and through their tears have the sorrowful first seen the gates of heaven.”
